Artificial Intelligence presents an enormous opportunity to the UK. It is at the heart of the UK’s plan to kickstart an era of economic growth, transform how public services are delivered and boost living standards for working people across the country. AI also introduces serious security risks that must be addressed to build public trust and ensure safe adoption.

items.t: Cheating behaviour in frontier model evaluations
items.why: Every model AISI tested tried to cheat on its cyber evaluations, by exploiting the task or environment; describes how cheating was detected and what it means for eval validity.
items.ab: We find cheating behaviour in all of our cyber capability evaluations, and outline the implications as models grow more capable. Can you trust an AI model to do what you intended? This is a central question both for those deploying AI systems and for those seeking to evaluate their capabilities. In deployment, a model that pursues a goal through unintended or unauthorised means may cause harm, particularly in high-stakes use cases.

items.t: An alignment safety case sketch based on debate
items.a: Marie Davidsen Buhl, Jacob Pfau, Benjamin Hilton et al.
items.why: Sketches an alignment safety case for an AI research agent trained with debate, identifying the open problems each argument step depends on.
items.ab: If AI systems match or exceed human capabilities on a wide range of tasks, it may become difficult for humans to efficiently judge their actions -- making it hard to use human feedback to steer them towards desirable traits. One proposed solution is to leverage another superhuman system to point out flaws in the system's outputs via a debate. This paper outlines the value of debate for AI safety, as well as the assumptions and further research required to make debate work.

items.t: Lessons from a Chimp: AI "Scheming" and the Quest for Ape Language
items.a: Christopher Summerfield, Lennart Luettgau, Magda Dubois et al.
items.why: Critiques AI-scheming research by analogy with 1970s ape-language studies: anecdotes, anthropomorphic interpretation and missing controls, with recommendations for rigour.
items.ab: We examine recent research that asks whether current AI systems may be developing a capacity for "scheming" (covertly and strategically pursuing misaligned goals). We compare current research practices in this field to those adopted in the 1970s to test whether non-human primates could master natural language.

items.t: Estimating Tail Risk in Neural Networks
items.why: Proposes estimating the probability of catastrophic outputs without finding the bad inputs, by reasoning about activations layer by layer, as a complement to adversarial training.
items.ab: Machine learning systems are typically trained to maximize average-case performance. However, this method of training can fail to meaningfully control the probability of tail events that might cause significant harm. For instance, while an artificial intelligence (AI) assistant may be generally safe, it would be catastrophic if it ever suggested an action that resulted in unnecessary large-scale harm. Current techniques for estimating the probability of tail events are based on finding inputs on which an AI behaves catastrophically.

items.t: Program Equilibrium in the Prisoner's Dilemma via Löb's Theorem
items.a: Patrick LaVictoire, Benja Fallenstein, Eliezer Yudkowsky et al.
items.why: Programs that read each other's source can achieve robust mutual cooperation in a one-shot prisoner's dilemma using provability logic (FairBot, PrudentBot).

items.t: Complex Value Systems are Required to Realize Valuable Futures
items.why: Argues human value is complex and fragile, so simple goal systems would produce worthless futures; the basis of the "value is fragile" thesis.

items.t: AI Governance to Avoid Extinction: The Strategic Landscape and Actionable Research Questions
items.why: MIRI's Technical Governance Team describes four geopolitical scenarios for advanced AI, favours building infrastructure for an internationally coordinated "off switch", and catalogues governance research questions.
items.ab: Humanity appears to be on course to soon develop AI systems that substantially outperform human experts in all cognitive domains and activities. We believe the default trajectory has a high likelihood of catastrophe, including human extinction. Risks come from failure to control powerful AI systems, misuse of AI by malicious rogue actors, war between great powers, and authoritarian lock-in. This research agenda has two aims: to describe the strategic landscape of AI development and to catalog important governance research questions.

items.t: An International Agreement to Prevent the Premature Creation of Artificial Superintelligence
items.a: Aaron Scher, David Abecassis, Peter Barnett et al.
items.why: A draft international agreement, led by the US and China, to halt premature superintelligence: FLOP limits on training, AI-chip tracking, and restrictions on dangerous AI research, with verification.
items.ab: Many experts argue that premature development of artificial superintelligence (ASI) poses catastrophic risks, including the risk of human extinction from misaligned ASI, geopolitical instability, and misuse by malicious actors. This report proposes an international agreement to prevent the premature development of ASI until AI development can proceed without these risks. The agreement halts dangerous AI capabilities advancement while preserving access to current, safe AI applications.

items.t: Research Note: Our scheming precursor evals had limited predictive power for our in-context scheming evals
items.why: Apollo's own "early warning" precursor evals predicted later scheming-eval results poorly, a caution for safety frameworks that rely on precursor capabilities.
items.ab: Note: This is a research note, and the analysis is less rigorous than our standard for a published paper. We’re sharing these findings because we think they might be valuable for other evaluators and decision-makers. In order to inform decision-makers early and track capabilities before the risks are realized, evaluators often build “early warning sign evals” that aim to measure precursor capabilities. Those precursors are intended to precede the capability of interest. If successful, this allows decision-makers to predict the dangerous capabilities ahead of time and prepare accordingly.

items.t: Evaluating and monitoring for AI scheming
items.a: Victoria Krakovna, Scott Emmons, Erik Jenner et al.
items.why: Summarises Google DeepMind's scheming strategy: stealth and situational-awareness evaluations plus chain-of-thought monitoring, and why current models seem unable to scheme undetected.
items.ab: As AI models become more sophisticated, a key concern is the potential for “deceptive alignment” or “scheming”. This is the risk of an AI system becoming aware that its goals do not align with human instructions, and deliberately trying to bypass the safety measures put in place by humans to prevent it from taking misaligned action. Our initial approach, as laid out in the Frontier Safety Framework, focuses on understanding current scheming capabilities of models and developing chain-of-thought monitoring mechanisms to oversee models once they are capable of scheming.

items.t: A Mike's-Eye View of ARC's Research
items.why: Updated 2026 picture of ARC's agenda after the Matching Sampling Principle: the concrete technical problems it generated and how they fit ARC's pipeline for aligning powerful AI.
items.ab: Over the past 15 months or so, ARC's technical agenda has developed quite a bit. The advent of the Matching Sampling Principle (MSP), and ideas like it, has begotten a host of concrete technical problems; progress on those problems has given us more philosophical clarity on the big picture, which has led to even more technical progress.

items.t: Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation
items.why: The standard reference on proper scoring rules: characterises them through convex functions and covers the Brier, log, CRPS, energy, interval and quantile scores.
items.ab: Scoring rules assess the quality of probabilistic forecasts, by assigning a numerical score based on the predictive distribution and on the event or value that materializes. A scoring rule is proper if the forecaster maximizes the expected score for an observation drawn from the distribution F if he or she issues the probabilistic forecast F, rather than G ≠ F. It is strictly proper if the maximum is unique.

items.t: Logarithmic Market Scoring Rules for Modular Combinatorial Information Aggregation
items.why: Introduced the logarithmic market scoring rule (LMSR), an automated market maker built from a proper scoring rule with a bounded subsidy; the basis of most later prediction-market market makers.
items.ab: In practice, scoring rules elicit good probability estimates from individuals, while betting markets elicit good consensus estimates from groups. Market scoring rules combine these features, eliciting estimates from individuals or groups, with groups costing no more than individuals. Regarding a bet on one event given another event, only logarithmic versions preserve the probability of the given event. Logarithmic versions also preserve the conditional probabilities of other events, and so preserve conditional independence relations.

items.t: Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness
items.a: Tilmann Gneiting, Fadoua Balabdaoui, Adrian E. Raftery
items.why: Introduced the principle "maximise sharpness subject to calibration" for evaluating forecast distributions, with tools such as PIT histograms and marginal calibration plots.
items.ab: Probabilistic forecasts of continuous variables take the form of predictive densities or predictive cumulative distribution functions. We propose a diagnostic approach to the evaluation of predictive performance that is based on the paradigm of maximizing the sharpness of the predictive distributions subject to calibration. Calibration refers to the statistical consistency between the distributional forecasts and the observations and is a joint property of the predictions and the events that materialize. Sharpness refers to the concentration of the predictive distributions and is a property…

items.t: Identifying and Cultivating Superforecasters as a Method of Improving Probabilistic Predictions
items.a: Barbara Mellers, Eric Stone, Terry Murray et al.
items.why: The Good Judgment Project's account of its winning strategy: putting the top 2% of forecasters into elite teams, where they kept their accuracy instead of regressing to the mean.
items.ab: Across a wide range of tasks, research has shown that people make poor probabilistic predictions of future events. Recently, the U.S. Intelligence Community sponsored a series of forecasting tournaments designed to explore the best strategies for generating accurate subjective probability estimates of geopolitical events. In this article, we describe the winning strategy: culling off top performers each year and assigning them into elite teams of superforecasters. Defying expectations of regression toward the mean 2 years in a row, superforecasters maintained high accuracy across hundreds of…

items.t: Shall We Vote on Values, But Bet on Beliefs?
items.why: The founding paper on futarchy: voters define a measure of national welfare and speculative markets choose the policies expected to raise it; works through 33 design issues.
items.ab: Democracies often fail to aggregate information, while speculative markets excel at this task. We consider a new form of governance, wherein voters would say what we want, but speculators would say how to get it. Elected representatives would oversee the after-the-fact measurement of national welfare, while market speculators would say which policies they expect to raise national welfare. Using a qualitative engineering-style approach, we present three scenarios, consider thirty-three design issues, and finally a more specific design responding to those concerns.

items.t: Prediction Markets
items.why: The standard economics introduction to prediction markets: contract types, evidence on accuracy from election and other markets, and limits such as manipulation and thin trading.
items.ab: In July 2003, press reports began to surface of a project within the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), a research think tank within the Department of Defense, to establish a Policy Analysis Market that would allow trading in various forms of geopolitical risk. Proposed contracts were based on indices of economic health, civil stability, military disposition, conflict indicators and potentially even specific events. The concept was to discover whether trading in such contracts could help to predict future events and how connections between events were perceived. However, a…

items.t: Forecasting Existential Risks: Evidence from a Long-Run Forecasting Tournament
items.a: Ezra Karger, Josh Rosenberg, Zachary Jacobs et al.
items.why: 169 superforecasters and domain experts forecast risks to humanity to 2100 over months of structured debate; the groups disagreed widely, most of all on AI, and barely converged.
items.ab: The Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT) aimed to produce high-quality forecasts of the risks facing humanity over the next century by incentivizing thoughtful forecasts, explanations, persuasion, and updating from 169 forecasters over a multi-stage tournament. In this first iteration of the XPT, we discover points where historically accurate forecasters on short-run questions (superforecasters) and domain experts agree and disagree in their probability estimates of short-, medium-, and long-run threats to humanity from artificial intelligence, nuclear war, biological pathogens, and…

items.t: Dissolving the Fermi Paradox
items.a: Anders Sandberg, Eric Drexler, Toby Ord
items.why: Shows that replacing point estimates in the Drake equation with realistic uncertainty distributions gives a substantial probability that we are alone: a model case for propagating uncertainty.
items.ab: The Fermi paradox is the conflict between an expectation of a high ex ante probability of intelligent life elsewhere in the universe and the apparently lifeless universe we in fact observe. We show that this conflict arises from the use of Drake-like equations, which implicitly assume certainty regarding highly uncertain parameters. When the model is recast to represent realistic distributions of uncertainty, we find a substantial ex ante probability of there being no other intelligent life in our observable universe, and thus that there should be little surprise when we fail to detect any…

items.t: Combinatorial Information Market Design
items.why: Shows how market scoring rules let one market cover all combinations of many variables, avoiding thin-market problems, and works through representation and bookkeeping issues.
items.ab: Information markets are markets created to aggregate information. Combinatorial information markets would aggregate information on the entire joint probability distribution over many variables, by allowing bets on all variable value combinations. To achieve this, we want to overcome the thin market and irrational participation problems that plague standard information markets. Scoring rules avoid these problems, but instead suffer from opinion pooling problems in the thick market case. Market scoring rules avoid all these problems, by becoming automated market makers in the thick market case…

items.t: The Promise of Prediction Markets
items.a: Kenneth J. Arrow, Robert Forsythe, Michael Gorham et al.
items.why: A Science policy forum by 22 economists and legal scholars (including Arrow, Schelling, Shiller and Smith) asking US regulators to allow small-stakes prediction markets for research.
items.ab: The ability of groups of people to make predictions is a potent research tool that should be freed of unnecessary government restrictions.

items.t: Vox Populi
items.why: Galton's two-page Nature note on 787 guesses of an ox's weight at a country fair: the median guess, 1,207 lb, was within 1% of the true 1,198 lb. The classic wisdom-of-crowds result.

items.t: Are You Smarter Than a Random Expert? The Robust Aggregation of Substitutable Signals
items.why: Gives theoretical grounding for extremizing: averaging experts' forecasts and then pushing the average away from the prior by a constant factor gives a much better worst-case guarantee.
items.ab: This paper initiates the study of forecast aggregation in a context where experts' knowledge is chosen adversarially from a broad class of information structures. We show that under the projective substitutes condition, taking the average of the experts' forecasts improves substantially upon the strategy of trusting a random expert. We then consider a more permissive setting, in which the aggregator has access to the prior. We show that by averaging the experts' forecasts and then extremizing the average by moving it away from the prior by a constant factor, the aggregator's performance…

items.t: From Proper Scoring Rules to Max-Min Optimal Forecast Aggregation

items.t: Laplace's rule of succession
items.why: Derives Laplace's rule of succession and discusses when it is a sensible prior for events with little or no historical precedent.
items.ab: Laplace's rule of succession is a commonly used heuristic in forecasting the occurence of events which have little to no historical precedents. The basic problem setup is this: suppose you flip a coin with an unknown bias N=H+T times and get H heads and T tails. We want to infer something about the bias p of the coin from this information, where we define p to be the probability of the coin coming up heads. One obvious idea is to estimate p by ^p=H/(H+T). This works well if we have some decent number of heads and tails, but it fails badly in the edge case where the tosses are very…

items.t: A Proper Scoring Rule for Confidence Intervals
items.why: A simple scoring rule for confidence intervals (interval width plus 20 times the miss distance) that makes reporting your honest 90% interval optimal.
items.ab: You probably already know that you can incentivise honest reporting of probabilities using a proper scoring rule like log score, but did you know that you can also incentivize honest reporting of confidence intervals? To incentize reporting of a 90% confidence interval, take the score −S−20⋅D, where S is the size of your confidence interval, and D is the distance between the true value and the interval. D is 0 whenever the true value is in the interval. This incentivizes not only giving an interval that has the true value 90% of the time, but also distributes the remaining 10% equally…

items.t: Relationship to Existing Approaches
items.why: Where delegation engineering sits relative to AI Control, frontier safety frameworks, FAIR, safety cases, agent-security patterns, scalable oversight, insurance and principal–agent theory, and what it actually adds.

items.t: Research
items.why: Background reading for the framework — literature reviews of the AI-safety evidence, surveys of precedents from other fields, and the list of open problems. Non-canonical; definitions live in the Delegation Risk section.

items.t: Open Problems in Delegation Engineering
items.why: A worklist for delegation engineering applied to AI agent systems: the open problems whose first results would tell us whether the framework holds — a preflight prototype, replicated monitor and correlation measurements on agentic harm tasks, multi-tenant entanglement, and more.

items.t: Principal–Agent Foundations
items.why: How delegation risk relates to the economics of delegation: agency costs, moral hazard and the informativeness principle, the multitask result, insurance, ambiguity aversion, and the standard assumptions that AI agents break.

items.t: Risk Budgeting and Tail Measures
items.why: How banks allocate a firm-wide risk limit: coherent risk measures, Euler and Shapley allocation, risk-appetite cascades, the failures of LTCM, 2008 and risk parity, and which parts apply to delegation risk.

items.t: Access Control Systems
items.why: What intelligence-community and enterprise access control teach about delegating authority to AI agents: compartmentation, need-to-know, two-person rules, permission sprawl, the confused deputy, and OAuth-style delegated authorization.

items.t: Mechanism Design
items.why: What incentive-compatible reporting can and cannot deliver for delegation risk: the revelation principle, VCG and its impossibility results, the multitask warning, and tools for eliciting honest probabilities.

items.t: Safety-Critical Engineering Precedents
items.why: How nuclear, aviation, process-industry and automotive safety engineering decompose a system-level target across components, where those methods break, and what transfers to AI delegation.

items.t: Formal Verification Limits for AI Systems
items.why: What can be proved about neural networks and AI systems, what cannot, where runtime verification and statistics take over, and why the provable part of a delegation design is the scaffold rather than the model.

items.t: Steganography and Encoded Reasoning in LLM Systems
items.why: Covert channels between language-model components: the threat model, information-theoretic capacity bounds, paraphrasing and other defences, and what 2023–25 experiments show current models can do.

items.t: Empirical Scheming Reduction
items.why: What propensity studies, evaluation-awareness work, control evaluations, monitor benchmarks, reasoning monitors and sandbagging audits have measured about scheming AI through late 2026, organised by the delegation-risk parameter each result informs.
